rv.q: The British comedy troupe Mischief Theatre has created a show that is both a loving parody of amateur theatricals and a masterpiece of physical comedy timing.
What's remarkable about this British import is how the company executes with such precision what amounts to 90 minutes of sustained slapstick.
For much of the night, you feel like you are watching the luckiest Broadway imposters in the world, and you probably are.
That Goes Wrong is a theatrical machine designed to generate laughs through spectacular failure, and it works with clockwork precision.
Under the go-for-broke direction of Mark Bell, its high-energy cast is comic gold.
It’s so ridiculous it makes you feel almost ashamed to love it.

An overabundance of non-sensical sight gags, slow burns, pratfalls, missed cues, wink-winks and the like dull the viewer’s senses and drag out a sophomoric sketch that would be sharper and funnier at an intermissionless 80 minutes.
Everything is pitched so aggressively, you wind up feeling as battered as the ensemble.
Depending on your tolerance for ceaseless slapstick, That Goes Wrong will either have you rolling in the aisles or rolling your eyes.
Long before the red herrings had been sorted out I came to feel that it wasn’t just the play-within-the-play that was going wrong, but the whole exhausting, exhausted conceit.
But for all the strenuous effort involved, the repetitive show evaporates in your mind the moment it concludes.
You only realize you've been smiling, gasping, and laughing for nearly two hours when it comes to not smiling upon your return to the regular world.
All told, That Goes Wrong goes uproariously right.
The eight performers have individual personalities but come together to form a tight ensemble well-disciplined in the art of being hilariously bad.
That Goes Wrong is just right: A ridiculously entertaining disaster.
There is NOTHING wrong with That Goes Wrong.
For much of its two-hour running time, “That Goes Wrong” offers a hilarious tribute to the spirit of the theater and the mantra that the show must go on — served up with a thick slice of ham.
As things stand, for me at least, a comedy this tired just can’t be right.
A comedy that comes up short with laughs and overstays its welcome — now that’s murder.

tn.cat: Best Scenic Design of a Play

cn.t: Critics mostly embrace this West End import's meticulously executed slapstick chaos, though some find the broad farce exhaustingly silly. Precision physical comedy and sustained laughs win over most reviewers.

sg.ra: Center orchestra rows D-G offer head-on sightlines to the high stage without neck strain. Gentle rake; intimate 922-seat house means even mid-orchestra feels close. Playbill notes Oh, Mary! action is downstage center, rewarding central seats.

Telecharge lists extreme sides of the first 11 orchestra rows as obstructed-view seats per Playbill. SeatPlan confirms double-digit seats are angled with far-side stage obstruction. 1903 house geometry leaves sharp side angles near stage.

sg.n: Orchestra Rear (Rows L-O, behind mezz overhang)
sg.ra: TickPick and SeatPlan both confirm Mezzanine overhang begins at Row L of Orchestra. AVFMS reviewer for O12 praised tiered rake ('raised above the row in front so you don't have any heads blocking you'). Fine for plays; top-of-stage cutoff limits tall-set musicals.

SeatPlan: 'patrons can look directly down to the stage, taking advantage of the Mezzanine's fantastic aerial views which don't sacrifice detail.' Excellent rake prevents blocked views. Ideal for spectacle/musicals where staging composition matters.

Folliesbroadway and Headout both flag Mezz D-F center as best value: clean sightlines, excellent rake, priced materially below front-mezz/prime-orchestra. Balcony overhang doesn't cut in until Row C so D-F also sit past the cutoff line without being affected (SeatPlan note is about row C).

sg.n: Mezzanine Rear (behind Row C — balcony overhang) and Side Double-Digits
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'Balcony overhang kicks in at row C, so views behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Double-digit side seats (D24, G22) have partial sightlines. Fine for plays; poor for tall scenic musicals.

Rows B and C clear the Row A safety rail and preserve a steep but clean center view. Tripadvisor: 'Great view of the stage, although a bit of an angled view down.' Starting prices on SeatPlan as low as $68-$80. Steep rake is uncomfortable but preserves sightlines.

sg.n: Balcony Row A and Side L/R front rows
sg.ra: Row A front has a safety rail that cuts across the stage (SeatPlan, Playbill, Tripadvisor all independently confirm). TickPick: Balcony L and R first two rows have partial views due to railing. Shorter patrons especially affected.
